questions.title: A cut pendulum and an uphill collision
questions.subtopic: A cut pendulum and an uphill collision
questions.stem: A $0.300\,\mathrm{kg}$ pendulum bob on a light $1.25\,\mathrm m$ string is released from rest at $60.0^\circ$ to the downward vertical. At the lowest point the string is cut immediately before the bob collides horizontally with a stationary $0.450\,\mathrm{kg}$ trolley. The bob sticks to the trolley, and the combined mass moves onto a frictionless ramp. Air resistance and rolling losses are negligible. Take $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Pendulum drop, bottom tension and a sticking collision

questions.changeNotes: Uses a non-horizontal release and unequal trolley mass, cuts the string explicitly and separates collision/ramp energy budgets.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Track changing system boundaries and use the appropriate conservation law at each stage.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Bob speed = 3.501785259 m s^-1; Bottom tension = 5.886 N; Post-impact speed = 1.400714104 m s^-1; Ramp height = 0.1 m; Collision energy-loss fraction = 0.6 ; Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: Energy is conserved on each lossless path but not as mechanical energy across sticking; cutting the string makes horizontal impulse conditions explicit.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the bob’s speed immediately before the string is cut.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the string tension immediately before it is cut.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the maximum vertical height reached by the combined bob and trolley, measured from the collision level.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why horizontal momentum is conserved during the short collision although mechanical energy is not.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of the bob’s pre-collision kinetic energy dissipated in the collision.

steps.text: The vertical drop is $h=L(1-\cos60^\circ)=0.625\,\mathrm m$, and $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$.
At the bottom, $T-mg=mv^2/L$; centripetal force is the resultant, not an additional force.
Horizontal momentum gives $0.300v=(0.300+0.450)u$.
$u=1.40\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ after sticking.
On the lossless ramp, $\tfrac12Mu^2=MgH$, so $H=u^2/(2g)=0.100\,\mathrm m$. Accept a consistent follow-through from part (a).
The string has been cut and external horizontal impulse during the short collision is negligible; the bob–trolley system’s horizontal momentum is conserved.
Sticking is inelastic: mechanical energy transfers to internal energy/deformation/sound. These transfers do not require loss of total energy.
$K_f/K_i=m_\mathrm{bob}/(m_\mathrm{bob}+m_\mathrm{trolley})=0.400$, so the dissipated fraction is $0.600$.

questions.answerSummary: a: $v=\sqrt{2(9.81)(0.625)}=3.50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.; b: $T=0.300[9.81+(3.5018)^2/1.25]=5.89\,\mathrm N$.; c: On the lossless ramp, $\tfrac12Mu^2=MgH$, so $H=u^2/(2g)=0.100\,\mathrm m$. Accept a consistent follow-through from part (a).; d: Sticking is inelastic: mechanical energy transfers to internal energy/deformation/sound. These transfers do not require loss of total energy.; e: $K_f/K_i=m_\mathrm{bob}/(m_\mathrm{bob}+m_\mathrm{trolley})=0.400$, so the dissipated fraction is $0.600$.

questions.title: Freezing water without cooling the final mixture
questions.subtopic: Freezing water without cooling the final mixture
questions.stem: Ice of mass $0.180\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $250\,\mathrm K$ is put into a large stirred ice–water mixture at $273\,\mathrm K$. The combined system is insulated, the container heat capacity is negligible, and enough liquid water remains that final equilibrium is at $273\,\mathrm K$. Use ice specific heat capacity $c=2100\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and latent heat of fusion $L_f=3.34\times10^5\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. For a solid with constant $c$, the entropy change between temperatures is supplied as $\Delta S=mc\ln(T_f/T_i)$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Ice warming by freezing water and entropy accounting

questions.changeNotes: Supplies the varying-temperature entropy expression, introduces a comparison repeat and explicitly defines the isolated system.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Distinguish thermal kinetic and potential energy and compare irreversible entropy budgets.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Heat gained by cold ice = 8694 J; Frozen liquid mass = 0.02602994012 kg; Ice entropy increase = 33.26811163 J K^-1; Water entropy decrease = -31.84615385 J K^-1; First total entropy increase = 1.421957782 J K^-1; Near-equilibrium repeat entropy = 0.02299192468 J K^-1

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the mass of liquid water that freezes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the freezing water loses internal energy while its temperature remains constant.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the entropy increase of the initially cold ice.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the total entropy change of the combined system and explain its consistency with the second law.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: In a repeat, the same ice mass starts at $270\,\mathrm K$. Calculate the new total entropy change and explain why it differs from part (d).

steps.text: The cold ice requires $Q=mc(273-250)=0.180(2100)(23)=8694\,\mathrm J$. The freezing water supplies this latent energy.
Temperature reflects mean random kinetic energy, which does not decrease during the equilibrium phase change.
Intermolecular potential energy decreases as the solid structure forms; the released latent energy warms the initially colder ice. Thus constant temperature does not imply constant internal energy.
Apply the supplied relationship to the warming ice, not $Q/273$ for the whole varying-temperature process.
The water freezes at $273\,\mathrm K$, so $\Delta S_\mathrm{water}=-8694/273=-31.8\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Total entropy increases by about $1.42\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.
The isolated combined system has positive entropy production from energy transfer across a finite temperature difference; one component may lose entropy while the total increases.
The initial temperature difference is much smaller, so the energy transfer is closer to reversible and produces less entropy. Both totals remain positive.

questions.answerSummary: a: $m_f=Q/L_f=8694/(3.34\times10^5)=0.0260\,\mathrm{kg}$.; b: Intermolecular potential energy decreases as the solid structure forms; the released latent energy warms the initially colder ice. Thus constant temperature does not imply constant internal energy.; c: $\Delta S_\mathrm{ice}=0.180(2100)\ln(273/250)=33.3\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.; d: The isolated combined system has positive entropy production from energy transfer across a finite temperature difference; one component may lose entropy while the total increases.; e: The initial temperature difference is much smaller, so the energy transfer is closer to reversible and produces less entropy. Both totals remain positive.

questions.title: A backward photon in two inertial frames
questions.subtopic: A backward photon in two inertial frames
questions.stem: A rocket passes a space station at event O and then moves in the positive $x$ direction at constant speed. The diagram uses the station frame S, with $x$ and $ct$ both in light-years. Event E on the rocket has coordinates $(x,ct)=(3.0,5.0)\,\mathrm{ly}$. At E the rocket emits a photon towards the station, which remains at $x=0$. The rocket frame S′ shares event O as its origin. Use $x^{\prime}=\gamma(x-\beta ct)$ and $ct^{\prime}=\gamma(ct-\beta x)$, where $\beta=v/c$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Rocket spacetime axes, backward light worldline and event transformations

questions.changeNotes: Replaces tilted-axis scale reading with explicitly scaled unprimed coordinates and adds a simultaneity comparison.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Keep event positions, frame synchronization and proper-time interpretations distinct.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Rocket Lorentz factor = 1.25 ; Photon arrival ct = 8 ly; Photon invariant interval = 0 ly^2; E rocket spatial coordinate = 0 ly; E rocket time = 4 yr; F rocket spatial coordinate = -6 ly; F rocket time = 10 yr; Relativity-of-simultaneity difference = 2.25 yr

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine $\beta$ and $\gamma$ for the rocket.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the station-frame coordinates of the photon’s arrival F and the spacetime interval $s^2=(\Delta ct)^2-(\Delta x)^2$ between E and F.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Transform E into S′ and identify the elapsed time on the rocket clock from O to E.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Transform F into S′. Explain why its time coordinate is not a reading made by the rocket’s clock at F.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Event G occurs at the station and is simultaneous with E in S. Determine whether G is earlier or later than E in S′, and by how much.

steps.text: The backward photon travels $3.0\,\mathrm{ly}$, so $F:(x,ct)=(0,8.0)\,\mathrm{ly}$.
$\Delta ct=3.0\,\mathrm{ly}$ and $\Delta x=-3.0\,\mathrm{ly}$, so $s^2=0\,\mathrm{ly^2}$; the interval is lightlike.
The rocket clock reads an elapsed proper time $4.0\,\mathrm{yr}$ because O and E both occur at $x^{\prime}=0$.
F is at $x^{\prime}=-6.0\,\mathrm{ly}$, not at the rocket clock. Its time is the S′ coordinate time assigned by synchronized clocks in that frame; the rocket clock does not pass through F.
G is later than E by $(6.25-4.0)\,\mathrm{yr}=2.25\,\mathrm{yr}$ in S′, despite simultaneity in S.

questions.answerSummary: a: $\gamma=(1-0.600^2)^{-1/2}=1.25$.; b: $\Delta ct=3.0\,\mathrm{ly}$ and $\Delta x=-3.0\,\mathrm{ly}$, so $s^2=0\,\mathrm{ly^2}$; the interval is lightlike.; c: The rocket clock reads an elapsed proper time $4.0\,\mathrm{yr}$ because O and E both occur at $x^{\prime}=0$.; d: F is at $x^{\prime}=-6.0\,\mathrm{ly}$, not at the rocket clock. Its time is the S′ coordinate time assigned by synchronized clocks in that frame; the rocket clock does not pass through F.; e: G is later than E by $(6.25-4.0)\,\mathrm{yr}=2.25\,\mathrm{yr}$ in S′, despite simultaneity in S.

questions.title: Overlapping orders of a broad spectrum
questions.subtopic: Overlapping orders of a broad spectrum
questions.stem: A diffraction grating has $500\,\mathrm{lines\,mm^{-1}}$. Light covering all wavelengths from $400\,\mathrm{nm}$ to $700\,\mathrm{nm}$ is incident normally. A distant flat screen is perpendicular to the undeviated beam. Use $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Broadband grating order widths and limiting complete order

questions.changeNotes: Uses a different grating and adds wavelength/order ambiguity and a monochromatic count.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Combine angular diffraction, integer order limits and spectral overlap.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Grating spacing = 2e-06 m; Second-order violet angle = 23.57817848 degree; Second-order red angle = 44.427004 degree; Second-order angular width = 20.84882552 degree; Highest complete order = 2 ; Third-order overlap wavelength = 440 nm; Overlap angle = 41.29987279 degree; Monochromatic observable maxima = 7

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the grating spacing in metres.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the angular width of the complete second-order spectrum.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the highest order containing the whole incident wavelength range, explaining the limiting wavelength.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: At one screen position, second-order $660\,\mathrm{nm}$ light overlaps third-order light. Determine the third-order wavelength and the diffraction angle.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The source is replaced by monochromatic $520\,\mathrm{nm}$ light. Determine the total number of diffraction maxima, including both sides and the central maximum, that can reach the screen.

steps.text: $\theta_\mathrm{violet}=\sin^{-1}[2(400\times10^{-9})/d]=23.58^\circ$ and $\theta_\mathrm{red}=\sin^{-1}[2(700\times10^{-9})/d]=44.43^\circ$.
The angular width is $44.43^\circ-23.58^\circ=20.85^\circ$. The width is a difference of inverse-sine angles, not the inverse sine of a wavelength difference.
The longest wavelength is most restrictive: $m\le d/(700\times10^{-9})=2.857$.
The highest complete order is $m=2$. Some shorter wavelengths appear in order 3, but the entire range does not.
At the same angle, $2\lambda_2=3\lambda_3$.
$m_{\max}=\lfloor d/(520\times10^{-9})\rfloor=3$; no grazing order is at the equality boundary for these data.
The total is $2m_{\max}+1=7$ maxima, at orders $0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$.

questions.answerSummary: a: $d=1/(500\times10^3)=2.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm m$.; b: The angular width is $44.43^\circ-23.58^\circ=20.85^\circ$. The width is a difference of inverse-sine angles, not the inverse sine of a wavelength difference.; c: The highest complete order is $m=2$. Some shorter wavelengths appear in order 3, but the entire range does not.; d: $\theta=\sin^{-1}[2(660\times10^{-9})/d]=41.30^\circ$.; e: The total is $2m_{\max}+1=7$ maxima, at orders $0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$.

questions.title: Which ion reaches the end of the plates?
questions.subtopic: Which ion reaches the end of the plates?
questions.stem: Horizontal plates of length $0.120\,\mathrm m$ are separated by $0.0400\,\mathrm m$ in a vacuum. Their potential difference is $320\,\mathrm V$, with the upper plate positive. A proton enters midway between them with horizontal velocity $3.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Edge fields and gravity are negligible. Use $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ and $m_p=1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Ion deflection between plates and crossed-field cancellation

questions.changeNotes: Changes all geometric/field data so both ions impact, asks for impact positions and distinguishes nominal continuation from real motion.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Test the physical boundary before using an exit formula, then compare charge-to-mass effects.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Electric field magnitude = 8000 V m^-1; Proton acceleration = 7.664670659e+11 m s^-2; Nominal proton deflection = 0.06131736527 m; Proton impact time = 2.28445836e-07 s; Proton impact distance = 0.06853375081 m; Nominal alpha deflection = 0.03065868263 m; Alpha impact distance = 0.09692135987 m; Crossed-field selector magnetic field = 0.02666666667 T

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the electric field strength and the proton’s vertical acceleration, including directions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine whether the proton reaches the far end of the plates. If it hits a plate first, determine the horizontal distance to impact.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: An alpha particle, of charge $+2e$ and mass $4m_p$, enters at the same point and speed. Determine whether it hits a plate.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A uniform magnetic field is added so that either ion at the stated speed passes undeflected. Determine its magnitude and direction.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: For an undeflected ion in the combined fields, state the net change in kinetic energy while it passes between the plates, with a reason.

steps.text: $E=V/s=320/0.0400=8.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, downwards from the positive plate.
$a_p=eE/m_p=7.66\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downwards.
The nominal transit time is $L/v=4.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm s$; unbounded vertical deflection would be $\tfrac12a_pt^2=0.0613\,\mathrm m>0.0200\,\mathrm m$, so the lower plate is hit.
Set $0.0200=\tfrac12a_pt_h^2$ to obtain $t_h=2.28\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm s$.
$x_h=vt_h=0.0685\,\mathrm m$, less than $0.120\,\mathrm m$. The nominal-exit deflection is a test, not an actual path beyond impact.
$a_\alpha=(2e)/(4m_p)\,E=a_p/2$. Its nominal-exit deflection is $0.0307\,\mathrm m$.
This still exceeds $0.0200\,\mathrm m$, so the alpha also hits the lower plate, at $x=\sqrt2\,x_h\approx0.0969\,\mathrm m$.
$qE=qvB$ gives $B=E/v=0.0267\,\mathrm T$, independent of ion charge-to-mass ratio.
B must be into the page: for positive charge moving right, the magnetic force is then upward and opposes the downward electric force.
The kinetic-energy change is zero. The net force vanishes, and the electric force is perpendicular to the straight trajectory; the magnetic force does no work.

questions.answerSummary: a: $a_p=eE/m_p=7.66\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, downwards.; b: $x_h=vt_h=0.0685\,\mathrm m$, less than $0.120\,\mathrm m$. The nominal-exit deflection is a test, not an actual path beyond impact.; c: This still exceeds $0.0200\,\mathrm m$, so the alpha also hits the lower plate, at $x=\sqrt2\,x_h\approx0.0969\,\mathrm m$.; d: B must be into the page: for positive charge moving right, the magnetic force is then upward and opposes the downward electric force.; e: The kinetic-energy change is zero. The net force vanishes, and the electric force is perpendicular to the straight trajectory; the magnetic force does no work.

questions.title: How far outside the tin nucleus?
questions.subtopic: How far outside the tin nucleus?
questions.stem: An alpha particle approaches a stationary tin nucleus head-on with initial kinetic energy $6.00\,\mathrm{MeV}$ when far away. The tin proton number is $50$, and its nucleon number is $120$. Neglect target recoil and assume electrostatic repulsion outside the nucleus. Use $ke^2=1.44\,\mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and $R=1.20A^{1/3}\,\mathrm{fm}$.

sourceAnchors.focus: Closest approach, isotope dependence, nuclear radius and high-energy departures

questions.changeNotes: Uses tin and two isotope masses, states no recoil explicitly and asks about distinct physical limits of the Coulomb model.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Separate proton-number and nucleon-number dependences and interpret a model’s validity range.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Tin closest-approach distance = 24 fm; Tin nuclear radius = 5.918908978 fm; Tin distance-radius ratio = 4.05480133 ; Isotope radius ratio = 1.013700333 ; Tin contact-energy scale = 24.32880798 MeV

questions.diagramSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 600 300" role="img"><circle cx="440" cy="150" r="45" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#edf2f4"/><text x="440" y="220" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">Sn nucleus</text><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="235" y2="150" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="235,150 225,146 225,154" fill="#17232b"/><circle cx="257.534" cy="150" r="6" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#17232b"/><line x1="257.534" y1="150" x2="440" y2="150" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text x="160" y="125" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">incoming alpha, 6.00 MeV</text><text x="345" y="130" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">d</text><line x1="440" y1="150" x2="485" y2="150" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="463" y="138" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">R</text><text x="300" y="270" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">Head-on; heavy target recoil neglected</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the distance of closest approach between the nuclear centres.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the tin nuclear radius and the ratio of closest approach to this radius.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The target is replaced by another tin isotope of nucleon number $125$. Explain how the predicted closest approach and nuclear radius change at the same incident alpha energy.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Estimate the alpha energy for which the electrostatic closest approach would equal the radius of the original $A=120$ nucleus.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons why the point-charge electrostatic description may fail once the closest-approach distance becomes comparable with the nuclear radius.

steps.text: At the head-on turning point, relative kinetic energy is zero and $K=k(2e)(50e)/d$.
$d=2(50)(1.44)/6.00=24.0\,\mathrm{fm}$. This is centre-to-centre distance.
Closest approach is unchanged in the stated no-recoil model because both isotopes have Z=50 and the incident energy is unchanged.
Radius increases by $(125/120)^{1/3}=1.014$, about $1.4\%$, because nuclear radius depends on nucleon number.
Set $d=R$ in the electrostatic energy relation, giving $K_\mathrm{est}=2Zke^2/R$.
$K_\mathrm{est}=144/5.92=24.3\,\mathrm{MeV}$. It is an estimate of a scale, not an exact threshold for every nuclear effect.
The target charge occupies a finite volume, so when the alpha penetrates that volume the outside point-charge potential no longer applies.

At nuclear separations the short-range strong nuclear interaction becomes important and electrostatic repulsion alone is insufficient. Accept a specific valid discussion of nuclear response/reactions; do not award a second mark for merely repeating that nuclei have a size.

questions.answerSummary: a: $d=2(50)(1.44)/6.00=24.0\,\mathrm{fm}$. This is centre-to-centre distance.; b: $d/R=24.0/5.92=4.05$.; c: Radius increases by $(125/120)^{1/3}=1.014$, about $1.4\%$, because nuclear radius depends on nucleon number.; d: $K_\mathrm{est}=144/5.92=24.3\,\mathrm{MeV}$. It is an estimate of a scale, not an exact threshold for every nuclear effect.; e: At nuclear separations the short-range strong nuclear interaction becomes important and electrostatic repulsion alone is insufficient. Accept a specific valid discussion of nuclear response/reactions; do not award a second mark for merely repeating that nuclei have a size.

questions.title: The turning point of an elastic safety cord
questions.subtopic: The turning point of an elastic safety cord
questions.stem: A $2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ test mass is released from rest at the fixed end of a light elastic safety cord. The cord is slack until the mass has fallen its unstretched length $1.60\,\mathrm m$. It then obeys Hooke’s law and reaches maximum extension $0.800\,\mathrm m$. Energy losses are negligible; use $g=10.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. A timer measures $0.205\,\mathrm s$ from the cord first becoming taut at A to the mass stopping at B.

sourceAnchors.focus: Free fall onto an elastic rope, energy and average tension

questions.changeNotes: Changes mass/length/extension, supplies a dynamically consistent timing measurement and tests an incorrect time-average argument.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Use whole-journey energy, turning-point dynamics and impulse without confusing time and extension averages.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Cord-taut speed = 5.656854249 m s^-1; Cord spring constant = 150 N m^-1; Turning-point acceleration = 50 m s^-2; Time-average cord force = 75.18882195 N; Ideal model stopping time rounds to sensor value = 0.205 s; Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: The measured 0.205 s is consistent with the exact spring response; average rope force exceeds half the peak because the mass spends more time at larger extension.

questions.diagramSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 600 300" role="img"><line x1="65" y1="45" x2="530" y2="45" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="125" cy="65" r="10" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#edf2f4"/><text x="125" y="100" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">release</text><line x1="300" y1="45" x2="300" y2="180" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><circle cx="300" cy="180" r="12" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#edf2f4"/><text x="300" y="220" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">A: just taut</text><line x1="475" y1="45" x2="475" y2="250" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="475" cy="250" r="12" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#edf2f4"/><text x="475" y="285" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">B: turning point</text><line x1="265" y1="45" x2="265" y2="180" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="220" y="125" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">1.60 m</text><line x1="520" y1="180" x2="520" y2="250" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="558" y="220" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">0.800 m</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed at A.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the cord’s spring constant.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude and direction of the acceleration at B. Explain why zero speed does not imply equilibrium.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Use impulse to calculate the average upward cord force between A and B.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A student estimates this average force as one half of the maximum cord force. Test that estimate and explain why a linear force–extension law does not justify it.

steps.text: Before A the mass falls freely, so $v_A^2=2gL$.
The full fall to B is $L+x=2.40\,\mathrm m$, so $mg(L+x)=\tfrac12kx^2$.
At B, $F_\mathrm{cord}=kx=120\,\mathrm N$ upward, giving resultant force $120-20=100\,\mathrm N$ and acceleration $50.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ upward.
B is an instantaneous turning point. Its velocity is zero but the forces do not balance, so it is not an equilibrium state.
Take upward positive: $(\overline F_\mathrm{cord}-mg)\Delta t=m[0-(-v_A)]$.
$\overline F_\mathrm{cord}=20.0+2.00(5.6569)/0.205=75.2\,\mathrm N$. Accept a consistent follow-through from part (a).
Half the maximum force is $60.0\,\mathrm N$, which does not match the impulse-derived $75.2\,\mathrm N$.
Hooke’s law makes force linear in extension, not linear in time. The changing velocity means extensions do not occupy equal time intervals, so the time average is not the midpoint of the force range.

questions.answerSummary: a: $v_A=\sqrt{2(10.0)(1.60)}=5.66\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ downwards.; b: $k=2(2.00)(10.0)(2.40)/(0.800)^2=150\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$.; c: B is an instantaneous turning point. Its velocity is zero but the forces do not balance, so it is not an equilibrium state.; d: $\overline F_\mathrm{cord}=20.0+2.00(5.6569)/0.205=75.2\,\mathrm N$. Accept a consistent follow-through from part (a).; e: Hooke’s law makes force linear in extension, not linear in time. The changing velocity means extensions do not occupy equal time intervals, so the time average is not the midpoint of the force range.

questions.title: Retuning two coherent water-wave sources
questions.stem: Two identical vertically oscillating drivers generate coherent water waves at S₁ and S₂. Each driver is a mass $0.160\,\mathrm{kg}$ on a spring of constant $64\pi^2\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. Initially they oscillate in phase at their natural frequency. The wave speed is constant at $1.50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At P the source distances are $2.40\,\mathrm m$ and $1.95\,\mathrm m$. Each wave alone has displacement amplitude $0.800\,\mathrm{mm}$ at the points considered; ignore damping and attenuation.

sourceAnchors.focus: Spring-driven coherent sources and next constructive-interference frequency

questions.changeNotes: Uses a different driver frequency, path order and next-node target; adds a controlled source-phase reversal at two positions.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Distinguish source phase, propagation phase and the direction of change of interference order.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Driver frequency = 10 Hz; Water wavelength = 0.15 m; P initial path order = 3 ; P first higher-frequency node = 11.66666667 Hz; Q path order = 3.5 ; Constructive amplitude = 1.6 mm

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial frequency of the drivers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the water wavelength.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the resultant amplitude at P, explaining the interference condition.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The drivers remain in phase while their common frequency is increased continuously. Determine the first frequency above the initial value for which P is a displacement node.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The initial frequency is restored, then one driver’s phase is reversed by half a cycle. State the resultant amplitudes at P and at Q, where the path difference is $0.525\,\mathrm m$, explaining the conditions.

steps.text: $f=(1/2\pi)\sqrt{k/m}$ for each ideal mass–spring driver.
Path difference is $2.40-1.95=0.450\,\mathrm m=3\lambda$, so initially in-phase waves arrive in phase.
Amplitudes add, giving $A_P=1.60\,\mathrm{mm}$.
For in-phase sources a node requires $\Delta r=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda=(n+\tfrac12)v/f$.
The initial path difference is three wavelengths. Increasing frequency increases $\Delta r/\lambda$, so the next node is at $3.5$, not $2.5$ wavelengths.
At P, the propagation phase difference is $6\pi$; adding the source phase reversal gives destructive interference, $A_P=0$.
At Q, $\Delta r/\lambda=0.525/0.150=3.5$. Its odd-π propagation phase difference is cancelled by the source phase reversal, so $A_Q=1.60\,\mathrm{mm}$.

questions.answerSummary: a: $f=(1/2\pi)\sqrt{64\pi^2/0.160}=10.0\,\mathrm{Hz}$.; b: $\lambda=v/f=1.50/10.0=0.150\,\mathrm m$.; c: Amplitudes add, giving $A_P=1.60\,\mathrm{mm}$.; d: $f=3.5(1.50)/0.450=11.7\,\mathrm{Hz}$.; e: At Q, $\Delta r/\lambda=0.525/0.150=3.5$. Its odd-π propagation phase difference is cancelled by the source phase reversal, so $A_Q=1.60\,\mathrm{mm}$.

questions.title: An escaping probe and a helium-burning star
questions.subtopic: An escaping probe and a helium-burning star
questions.stem:
A non-relativistic probe leaves an airless planet with speed $10.0\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. The escape speed from the launch point is $8.00\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. After launch only the planet’s gravity acts. Farther out on the same radial path, its speed decreases from $7.00\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ at P to $6.80\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ at Q over $3.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.

A separate helium-burning stellar core supports the reaction $3\,{}^4_2\mathrm{He}\rightarrow{}^{12}_6\mathrm C+\gamma$. Use atomic masses $m({}^4\mathrm{He})=4.00260\,\mathrm u$, $m({}^{12}\mathrm C)=12.00000\,\mathrm u$ and $1\,\mathrm u\,c^2=931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$. The atomic electron counts balance between reactants and products.

sourceAnchors.focus: Escape energy, average gravitational field and stellar fusion energy

questions.changeNotes: Uses a different launch/escape pair, asks for a true path-averaged field, and replaces the source reaction by explicitly balanced triple-alpha burning.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Separate gravitational energy bookkeeping from nuclear mass-energy and stellar mechanical equilibrium.

verification.method: Reproducible author calculation, dimensional and limiting-case checks
verification.notes: Asymptotic escape speed = 6 km s^-1; Path-average gravitational field = 0.46 N kg^-1; Triple-alpha mass defect = 0.0078 u; Triple-alpha energy release = 7.2657 MeV; Physical reasoning and distractor uniqueness: Escape and path-work calculations use supplied positions and infinity, with no numerical elliptical orbit/transfer assumptions. Atomic electron numbers balance 6 to 6.

questions.diagramSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 600 300" role="img"><circle cx="90" cy="155" r="55" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#edf2f4"/><text x="90" y="160" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">planet</text><line x1="145" y1="155" x2="540" y2="155" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><circle cx="280" cy="155" r="5" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#17232b"/><circle cx="475" cy="155" r="5" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2" fill="#17232b"/><line x1="290" y1="155" x2="350" y2="155" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="350,155 340,151 340,159" fill="#17232b"/><line x1="485" y1="155" x2="545" y2="155" stroke="#17232b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="545,155 535,151 535,159" fill="#17232b"/><text x="280" y="120" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">P: 7.00 km s⁻¹</text><text x="475" y="195" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">Q: 6.80 km s⁻¹</text><text x="375" y="250" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="#17232b">PQ = 3.00 × 10⁶ m</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the probe’s speed at a very large distance from the planet.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the gravitational field averaged along the path from P to Q, using work and energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy released in the stated fusion reaction.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why helium fusion requires higher core temperatures than fusion of hydrogen nuclei, and why fusion beyond the iron-group peak cannot provide a sustained stellar energy source.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Outline the mechanical condition for the stellar core to remain in hydrostatic equilibrium and how nuclear energy generation helps maintain that condition.

steps.text: With potential zero at infinity, the energy required for escape is $\tfrac12mv_\mathrm{esc}^2$. Thus $\tfrac12mv_0^2-\tfrac12mv_\mathrm{esc}^2=\tfrac12mv_\infty^2$.
The positive loss of kinetic energy per unit mass equals $\overline g\,s$: $\overline g=(v_P^2-v_Q^2)/(2s)$. This defines the path average even though g is not constant.
$\overline g=[7000^2-6800^2]/[2(3.00\times10^6)]=0.460\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ towards the planet.
The mass defect is $3(4.00260)-12.00000=0.00780\,\mathrm u$; balanced electron counts permit use of the supplied atomic masses.
$E=0.00780(931.5)=7.27\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per reaction.

Helium nuclei have greater positive charge than hydrogen nuclei, hence greater electrostatic repulsion; higher random kinetic energies/temperatures are required to approach closely enough for nuclear fusion.
Near the iron-group binding-energy-per-nucleon maximum, further fusion no longer gives a net increase in binding energy per nucleon and becomes energy-consuming, so it cannot sustain energy output.
The outward pressure-gradient force balances inward gravity locally; accept thermal and/or radiation pressure as appropriate.
Nuclear energy replenishes energy radiated away, maintaining core temperature and pressure support. Equilibrium does not mean gravity vanishes or that no energy flows outward.

questions.answerSummary: a: $v_\infty=\sqrt{10.0^2-8.00^2}=6.00\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.; b: $\overline g=[7000^2-6800^2]/[2(3.00\times10^6)]=0.460\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ towards the planet.; c: $E=0.00780(931.5)=7.27\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per reaction.; d: Near the iron-group binding-energy-per-nucleon maximum, further fusion no longer gives a net increase in binding energy per nucleon and becomes energy-consuming, so it cannot sustain energy output.; e: Nuclear energy replenishes energy radiated away, maintaining core temperature and pressure support. Equilibrium does not mean gravity vanishes or that no energy flows outward.
